Unofficial until approved by the
  Alhambra City Council

  MINUTES
  Regular Meeting
  ALHAMBRA CITY COUNCIL
  Ruth Reese Hall, 101 South First Street
  February 22, 2021
  6:00 p.m.

ROLL CALL: At 6:10 p.m., on Monday, February 22, 2021 the Alhambra City Council met via
video conference, and via teleconference.

COUNCIL PRESENT via video conference: LEE, MAZA, MALONEY, ANDRADE-STADLER,
PÉREZ
ABSENT:  NONE

Officials Present physically, via teleconference, and via video conference: City Manager
Binnquist, City Attorney Montes, Assistant City Manager Garcia, Deputy City Manager Tran,
City Clerk Myles, Director of Finance Lieu, Director of Public Works/ Utilities Ray, Director of
Parks and Recreation Macias, Management Analyst Cuevas, Director of Community
Development Castagnola, Fire Chief Phelps, Police Chief Vu, Director of Human Resources Ko

FLAG SALUTE:  Mayor Pérez

CITY CLERK REPORT - NOTICE NO. N2M21-19

The City Clerk reported that she duly gave notice of the regular meeting of the City Council
being held pursuant to the order of the Mayor in accordance with Section 54955 and 54956 of
the Government Code of the State of California.

CEREMONIAL

1.  CERTIFICATE OF SERVICE: CHIEF OF POLICE TIMOTHY VU – F2M21-3

  Mayor Pérez and the City Council wished to commend and thank Chief of Police
  Timothy Vu for his 4 years of faithful and loyal service to the Police Department and the
  City of Alhambra. Staff presented a Certificate of Service plaque to Chief Vu for his
  outstanding work for the City.

  Discussion: Chief VU expressed gratitude for Council, City staff, his fellow Police staff,
  and the community. Council continued to discuss the many programs implemented and
  led by Chief Vu and his dedication to helping the community.

PRESENTATIONS

2.  PRESENTATION BY THE BREATHE FREE ALHAMBRA COALITION & AMERICAN
  CANCER SOCIETY – F2M21-16

  1
2-22-21
   Guadulesa Rivera from the Breathe Free Alhambra Coalition and Primo Castro from the
  American Cancer Society presented information on the dangers of second-hand smoke
  in public places as well as smoking and youth addiction to nicotine, especially flavored
  vape. They discussed comprehensive policies and ordinances which would address
  limiting public smoking areas and the sale of flavored tobacco products. The
  presentation is on file in the City Clerk’s office.

  Public Comment:

  The following people spoke advocating for an updated and comprehensive
  ordinance to address outdoor smoking in public places and flavored tobacco
  products:

  1) Nicolas Kiet Quach, a student at Alhambra High School and a member of Alhambra
  Unified School District Tobacco Use Prevention Education Student Advocates

  2) Francis Ngo, a student at Martha Baldwin Elementary School and a member of
  Alhambra Unified School District Tobacco Use Prevention Education Student
  Advocates

  3) Sophie Lin, a student at San Gabriel High School and a member of Alhambra Unified
  School District Tobacco Use Prevention Education Student Advocates

  4) Linh Dinh, a student at San Gabriel High School and a member of Alhambra Unified
  School District Tobacco Use Prevention Education Student Advocates

  5) Vivian Dong, a student at Mark Keppel High School and a member of Alhambra
  Unified School District Tobacco Use Prevention Education Student Advocates

  6) Elizabeth Jacoby, representing the Los Angeles County Tobacco Control and
  Prevention Program, also discussed the implementation of a Tobacco Retail
  Licensing Program.

  7) Yixuan Gao, a student at Martha Baldwin Elementary School and a member of
  Alhambra Unified School District Tobacco Use Prevention Education Student
  Advocates

  8) Arwa Saleh, a student at Marth Baldwin Elementary School and a member of
  Alhambra Unified School District Tobacco Use Prevention Education Student
  Advocates

  Public Comment received via email on file in the City Clerk’s office: Sergio Rivera
  wrote regarding the health risks associated with second hand smoke exposure and
  advocated for an updated ordinance further limiting smoking in outdoor public areas.

  Discussion: Councilmember ANDRADE-STADLER discussed the current smoking
  City ordinance with Ms. RIVERA and Mr. CASTRO as it related to AUSD policies against
  smoking in school buildings. Ms. ANDRADE-STADLER went on to refer to comments
  made by students regarding tobacco companies targeting youth through flavored
  tobacco products and expressed her concerns as to the effects on youth. She went on to
  suggest that Council strengthen the current ordinance to be more comprehensive

  2
2-22-21
   regarding outdoor smoking as well as implementing a ban on retailers from selling
  flavored tobacco products within 3 – 6 months of adoption. Mr. CASTRO discussed
  similar local policies which the American Cancer Society helped other cities draft.

  Councilmember LEE discussed her background as a middle school teacher and
  expressed frustration in trying to educate and prevent children from using tobacco
  products. She continued to speak against electronic and vaping cigarettes, smoking
  addiction among youth, and retailers near schools which sell flavored tobacco products.
  She supported Ms. Andrade-Stadler’s suggestion of an ordinance banning the sale of
  flavored tobacco products.

  Councilmember MALONEY, Councilmember MAZA, and Mayor PÉREZ echoed
  previous comments regarding the risks of second-hand smoke and tobacco products
  and supported further discussion about updating current ordinances. Ms. PÉREZ also
  supported discussion of a Tobacco Retail Licensing Program to limit the number of new
  tobacco and vaping stores.

  Action Taken:  City Council received and filed the informational report, and
  directed Staff return with a report on the current State and Local smoking regulations as
  well as a menu of options for augmenting the City’s current ordinance regarding smoking
  prohibition areas and a new Tobacco Retail Licensing Program.

3.  SELECTION OF PROPOSALS RECEIVED FOR A POTENTIAL AFFORDABLE
  HOUSING PROJECT ON CHAPEL AVENUE – F2M20-71, RFP2M20-33, M2M21-23

  Director of Community Development CASTAGNOLA delivered a staff report and
  presentation which is available in the City Clerk’s office. On October 12, 2020, the City
  Council and the Successor Agency adopted a resolution approving an amendment to a
  Disposition and Development Agreement with Hillcrest Development Partners making a
  portion of public parking located at 103 N. Chapel Avenue available for the development
  of a second affordable housing project within the Central Business District. The site was
  utilized as an overflow surface parking lot to the main public parking structure with 46
  underutilized spaces. The parcel was about 0.31 acres (13,750 Sq. Ft.), but benefitted
  from the adjacent availability of the parking structure for the project parking needs. A
  Request for Proposals (RFP) sought to identify a qualified non-profit developer to
  provide a mix of low-income housing opportunity with contributing housing asset funds.
  The levels of affordability were not specified in the RFP and were left open to a wide
  range of income eligibility from supportive housing to moderate income in order for the
  developers to propose what they thought would be most financially feasible on that site
  and based on subsidies available in relationship to the type of product proposed. The
  RFP required developers to submit information such as the total number of proposed
  units and unit mix with respect to specific affordable income categories. By the
  submission deadline, the City received a total of seven proposals as follows (ranked by
  project height and then number of units): 1) Restore Neighborhoods LA (RNLA); 2)
  GANGI Development; 3) RELATED; 4) American Family Housing & National CORE; 5)
  Many Mansions; 6) Elsey Partners; and, 7) PFIC. Staff sought Council to select a
  Developer and associated project for staff to enter into an Exclusive Negotiation
  Agreement (ENA) similar to the ENA used for the Mariposa project with the Council’s
  selected developer. Concurrent with the ENA, City staff would contract with Keyser
  Marston and Associates (“KMA”), at the developer’s cost, for a peer review of the

  3
2-22-21
   selected developer’s pro-forma. KMA was a recognized real estate development
  consultant with extensive experience in affordable housing projects and has worked with
  the City in the past. The ENA would be in effect for 180 days, after which staff would
  bring a Disposition and Development Agreement (DDA) back to the Council for
  consideration.

  Public Comment received via email on file in the City Clerk’s office:

  1) Jose Luis ESPINOZA, Jr. wrote to request that the City discuss the possibility of the
  chosen developer commit to hiring local businesses.

  2) Sean MCMORRIS wrote to request that the project benefit the most people at
  income levels that were least represented in the City’s Affordable Housing
  Ordinance, suggest that Council select a developer with a track record of continued
  care after the project is built, and suggest Restore Neighborhoods LA or American
  Family Housing/National CORE as potential developers.

  3) Ana CORTES wrote in support of the project.

  4) Shirley TATSUNO wrote in support of RELATED and AFH/National Core as potential
  developers and went on to question the number of tenants allowed per unit.

  5) Lewis MCCAMMON wrote in support of the project focusing on a mix of units and
  include a strong emphasis on family units at the low-income level. He supported the
  consideration of American Family Housing and National CORE.

  Discussion: Councilmember LEE reported that she had previously received a tour of
  other projects by American Family Housing while reviewing their application for the
  Mariposa development and requested a tour of similar projects built by RELATED. Rose
  OLSON, representing RELATED, confirmed that Council would be able to visit other
  completed developments and went on to list recently completed projects of a similar size
  and scope to the proposed development on Chapel Avenue.

  Councilmember MALONEY and Mr. CASTAGNOLA discussed the competitive 4% or
  9% tax credit which would be awarded to the developer, the qualifications of the
  potential developers, and the potential City contribution should the developer not qualify
  for the tax credit. They further discussed the funding sources for the City’s contribution.

  Mayor Pérez allowed each of the development representatives five minutes to address
  Council and clarify points regarding their submitted proposals. Mr. Bryan ELSEY,
  representing Elsey Partners; Mr. Alexander RUSSELL, representing Man Mansions; Mr.
  Frank GANGI, representing GANGI Development; Mr. John PERFITT, representing
  Restore Neighborhood LA; Mr. Michael RUANE, representing American Family Housing/
  CORE; Ms. Rose OLSON, representing RELATED; and Mr. Keith MCCLOSKEY and
  Jeffrey TAMKIN, representing Public Facilities Investment Core (PFIC); spoke regarding
  the cost benefits of their proposals, achieving the optimum number of units and people
  per unit, other potential amenities, innovative design concepts, additional onsite services
  to families, efficient use of available funding sources and tax credit options, past project
  experience, the City’s needs and goals, prioritizing family housing, inclusivity and
  accessibility issues, financing structure for the project, use of tax exempt bonds, and Los

  4
2-22-21
   Angeles County and California affordable housing requirements.

  Mr. MALONEY continued to discuss tax credit system and suggested that dependant on
  the outcome of the selected developer’s application, that the City ensure that they would
  not have to make additional contributions to fill the funding gap. He further discussed the
  City’s land contribution with Mr. CASTAGNOLA and pending land appraisals. He agreed
  with Staff’s recommendations based on Council’s intentions and goals for the project to
  strike a balance in integrating a large development in the existing neighborhood. He felt
  that 4 or 5 stories was an appropriate height, agreed with the broad range of income
  levels while not exceeding 60% AMI, and agreed with the variety of units available. He
  spoke to previous discussions and his preference to provide housing to allow families to
  stay in Alhambra. He supported the American Family Housing proposal given the City’s
  history with them, but also supported the RELATED proposal for the variety of income
  groups and unit types proposed despite a higher City contribution. He praised the
  Restore Neighborhood LA proposal for its financial creativity but added that he felt it
  didn’t provide enough units. He discussed energy efficiency, the inclusion of solar
  panels, and LEED ratings in the American Family Housing and RELATED proposals with
  Mr. CASTAGNOLA, Ms. OLSON, and Mr. RUANE. He encouraged the potential
  developers to continue to consider the overall project cost while still attempting to
  achieve a high LEED status as well as communicating with the Clean Power Alliance to
  research programs which may help bring down energy costs.

  Councilmember MAZA thanked staff for the comprehensive report, all developers who
  submitted proposals, and agreed with staff’s recommendations of American Family
  Housing or RELATED. Mr. MAZA and Mr. CASTAGNOLA discussed the inclusion of
  permanent supportive housing, the project timeline with regards to the developer
  acquiring bonds and the cap on the City’s contribution to the project, public review of the
  proposal, Council’s approval process, and the inclusion of special needs units for the
  homeless. Mr. MAZA supported the proposal from RELATED given the more balanced
  mix of units to provide housing for families.

  Councilmember ANDRADE-STADLER thanked the developers for their proposals to
  address the needs of the community and referred to previous conversations with the
  public regarding the need for affordable housing and to consider family appropriate
  housing. She supported the proposal from RELATED given the mix of units to
  accommodate families and the 5-story limit which would be appropriate for the
  neighborhood. She agreed with Mr. Maloney’s suggestions regarding energy efficiency
  and connecting to greenspace. She suggested a local hiring preference and discussed
  the possibility with Ms. OLSON.

  Ms. PÉREZ thanked the developers and agreed with Mr. Maza and Ms. Andrade-Stadler
  in their support of the RELATED proposal and their inclusion of family appropriate units.
  She also agreed with Mr. Maloney’s energy efficiency suggestions and Ms. Olson’s
  positive response. She further agreed with Ms. Olson’s comments regarding local hiring
  process.

  Action Taken:  City Council received the presentation of all respondents to the
  Request for Proposals (RFP) for an affordable housing project on Chapel Avenue and
  directed staff to enter into an Exclusive Negotiation Agreement (ENA), similar to the
  agreement used for the Mariposa project, with RELATED. (M2M21-23)

  5
2-22-21
   Vote:  Moved:  ANDRADE-STADLER  Seconded: MAZA
  Ayes:  MALONEY, MAZA, LEE, ANDRADE-STADLER, PÉREZ
  Noes:  NONE
  Absent:  NONE

4.  DIRECTION ON RESTRUCTURING ALHAMBRA’S BOARDS, COMMISSIONS AND
  COMMITTEES – F2M20-34

  Assistant City Manager GARCIA delivered a staff report. The City of Alhambra has ten
  advisory boards, commissions and committees. The establishment of these groups are
  authorized under Chapter Two of the City’s Municipal Code, which states in part that
  Boards and Commissions shall be established to enhance public engagement in the City’s
  decision-making process. Pursuant to the Code, the City Council has the ultimate authority
  to establish, modify, or sunset the boards and commissions at any time, as it deems
  necessary. The City’s 2020-21 Strategic Plan includes Goal 12 relative to Restructuring the
  City’s Boards and Commissions. Under this Goal, the City aimed to restructure these
  groups commensurate with the Council’s priorities, including efficiency, effectiveness, and
  ongoing public engagement. Ms. Garcia presented considerations or rationale for possibly
  changing the existing board and commission structures as well as suggestions for various
  restructuring alternatives for the Council’s consideration.

  Public Comment:

  1) Michael LAWRENCE opposed the limits on Planning Commission members and
  requirements for Design Review Board Members.

  2) Chris OLSON opposed establishing requirements for Planning Commission and
  Design Review Board members and suggested a re-education of the current
  members.

  3) Meghan WEBSTER, a member of the Youth Commission, opposed changes to the
  Youth Commission but use it to enhance youth engagement.

  Public Comment received via email on file in the City Clerk’s office:

  The following people wrote against proposed changes to the boards and
  commissions regarding decreasing number of appointed positions and imposing
  membership requirements:

  1)  Jose Luis Espinoza
  2)  Melissa Michelson
  3)  Cliff Bender
  4)  Yvette Cardenas
  5)  Lewis McCammon, who also suggested the inclusion of an Historic Preservation
  Committee

  Discussion: Councilmember LEE suggested that the roles of Board and Commission
  members be better defined. She related a discussion with Ms. Webster and her mother
  and stressed the importance of youth involvement and participation in government. She

  6
2-22-21
   spoke regarding the HCDA Advisory Board, their capacity to offer input to Council, and
  Council’s opportunity to provide involvement in City government. She suggested a
  charter for the Environmental Committee to better address the City’s goals for
  sustainability. Regarding the suggested requirements for Planning Commission and
  Design Review Board, Ms. Lee stressed the importance of Council making appointments
  based on representation and opposed the suggested requirements and reduction of
  members. She referred to Ms. Webster’s comments regarding the Youth Commission’s
  ability to assist the senior community and opposed eliminating the commission. She
  suggested that after the COVID restrictions were lifted, that the Youth Commission
  become more involved and move under the supervision of the Library Director given the
  library’s familiarity with youth centered programs. Ms. Lee supported providing further
  training for Planning Commission and Design Review Board members rather than
  education requirements.

  Councilmember MALONEY referred to discussions at the previous year’s Strategic
  Planning session and stressed the need for additional discussion about increasing public
  input in the government. He discussed possible new commissions and suggested a
  Historic Preservation Commission and a Budget Advisory Commission. He supported a
  review of the scope and duties of each commission. He agreed with Ms. Lee’s
  comments and suggested that the Environmental Committee be repurposed and
  renamed as the Sustainability Committee. He further expressed hesitancy to put
  education requirements on the qualifications of Planning Commission and Design
  Review Board members and supported providing education to new commissioners. Mr.
  Maloney considered the reduction of Planning Commission members and discussed the
  difficulties in managing complex agendas and making efficient judicial decisions. He
  discussed other cities which appoint five members and stressed that a reduction of
  members be considered in conjunction with expanding the scope of existing
  commissions, creating new commissions, and expanding opportunities overall for civic
  input. He further related his discussion with past and present Planning Commissioners
  regarding negative experiences as well as positive experiences of Design Review Board
  Members. He opposed education requirements but supported a robust education
  process for new members. He opposed recommendations to reduce other commissions
  and requested further discussion of the Youth Commission. He suggested reducing the
  members rather than eliminating the Youth Commission or the creation of appointed
  youth positions within other commissions. Mr. Maloney discussed the creation of a new
  advisory commission to address some of the concerns raised within Planning
  Commission meetings, creating alternating positions to address the lack of quorum, and
  the possibility of Council liaisons to each of the commissions.

  Councilmember ANDRADE-STADLER opposed any changes to boards and
  commissions. She related the benefit of receiving input from her commissioners,
  stressed the importance of representation on the Planning Commission, the high volume
  of work before the Planning Commission, and the importance of input from Planning
  Commissioners with and without professional backgrounds. She praised youth
  engagement and opposed eliminating the Youth Commission. She agreed with Mr.
  Maloney’s suggestion of Council liaisons and agreed to be a liaison to the Youth
  Commission. Ms. Andrade-Stadler opposed the elimination of the Environmental
  Committee and stressed the need for more greenspace. She further stressed the need
  for public engagement and disagreed with the suggestions for streamlining. She
  supported the creation of an Historic Preservation Commission and discussed
  addressing the status of women, children, and immigrants in the city.

  7
2-22-21
   Councilmember MAZA suggested further discussion in greater detail at the Strategic
  Planning session. He emphasized the need for community involvement and outreach.
  He acknowledged the reasoning behind the recommendations, but stressed the need for
  more training and guidance and to better define the roles of the boards and
  commissions. He opposed the education requirements and suggested appointments
  based on common sense and providing education and training to new appointees. Mr.
  Maza supported providing defined design guidelines for the Design Review Board and
  stressed the need for further discussion of the guidelines. He referred to discussions
  regarding Measure V, and suggested that Planning Commissioners and Design Review
  Board Members be appointed by district for better representation within those districts.
  He opposed the dissolution of the Youth Commission and stated that there should be
  further discussion of youth engagement. Mr. Maza additionally supported further
  discussion expanding the scope of the Arts and Cultural Events Committee.

  Mayor PÉREZ explained the staff report in terms of direction received by the previous
  Council at the Strategic Planning session, supported further discussion establishing the
  purpose of each commission, and went on to list topics which could direct Council’s
  discussion such as the desired experiences of commissioners, the charge of each
  commission, the continual work of each commission, number of cancelled meetings per
  commission, number of vacancies per commission, frequency of meetings, and the
  larger role of commissions within public service and Council business. She stressed the
  importance of youth representation not only in the Youth Commission, but as
  contributing partners in the community. She agreed with Mr. Maza’s suggestion of
  selecting commissioners by district as well as selecting commissioners from a variety of
  backgrounds as a way of ensuring more equitable representation. She suggested using
  language to guide Councilmembers in their appointments rather than provide
  restrictions. She supported the creation of a Citizen’s Academy to educate
  commissioners in the scope of the municipal government and the role of each
  commission. She supported further discussion at future Strategic Planning Sessions.

  Action Taken:  City Council received and filed the staff report.

5.  COUNCIL DIRECTION ON HERO PAY FOR GROCERY WORKERS – F2M20-33

  At the January 11, 2021 Council meeting, Mayor PÉREZ requested a discussion about
  Hero Pay for grocery workers. Hero Pay is generally an additional $4 per hour for
  grocery workers due to the greater risk of workplace COVID exposure. Other cities’
  ordinances apply to private and publicly owned grocery stores with over 300 employees
  nationwide and 10 employees locally, and Hero Pay is for a duration of 120 days. The
  County of Los Angeles was considering adoption of such an ordinance until the
  California Grocers Association announced it had filed a federal lawsuit against the City
  of Long Beach arguing the hazard pay is unconstitutional. A hearing on a preliminary
  injunction, which would stop the ordinance from taking effect while the case is pending,
  was set for February 19, but Ms. Pérez informed the Council it was postponed until
  February 23rd. In an attempt to avoid a similar legal circumstance, other cities are
  looking to make decisions after the Long Beach hearing. Conversely, some cities have
  moved forward with ordinances, notwithstanding the pending Long Beach lawsuit. Ms.
  Pérez stated that she would like to discuss the matter with her fellow Councilmembers,
  but acknowledged that outside events which may inform their decisions have yet to take

  8
2-22-21
   place and staff currently sought Council’s direction. Council unanimously agreed to
  move forward with the discussion. City Attorney MONTES provided a brief background
  report.

  Public Comment:

  1) Rachel TORRES supported the ordinance and submitted an additional letter to
  Council, which is on file in the City Clerk’s office.

  2) Randy GUITRON, Produce Manager at Albertsons, spoke regarding the added
  stress during the COVID-19 pandemic as a grocery store worker and spoke in favor
  of the ordinance.

  Public Comment received via email on file in the City Clerk’s office:

  The following people spoke in favor of the ordinance:

  1) Grecia Lopez-Reyes

  The following people spoke against the ordinance:

  1) Steve McCarthy, representing the California Retailers Association
  2) Kyle Griffith, of Bicker, Castillo & Fairbanks, representing California Grocers
  Association, Family Business Association of California, California Fuels &
  Convenience Alliance, California Black Chamber of Commerce, Long Beach Area
  Chamber of Commerce, Los Angeles Area Chamber of Commerce, Valley Industry &
  Commerce Association, Los Angeles County Business Federation, National Diversity
  Coalition, Si Se Puede Foundation of Fresno, Kern, Kings and Tulare Counties,
  California Retailers Association, Latino Food Industry Association, California
  Business Roundtable, CalAsian Chamber of Commerce, California Hispanic
  Chambers of Commerce, The Latin Business Association, Orange County Business
  Council, San Gabriel Valley Economic Partnership, Southwest California Legislative
  Council, and the Greater Riverside Chambers of Commerce
  3) Barbara Messina
  4) Timothy James, representing the California Grocers Association
  5) William F. Tarantino of Morrison & Forrester, representing the California Grocers
  Association

  Discussion:  Councilmember ANDRADE-STADLER discussed Council’s
  options, traditional labor negotiations versus the extenuating circumstances of the
  COVID-19 pandemic, pending vaccinations for essential workers who have continued to
  work despite their potential exposure to the virus, and ultimately supported continued
  discussion of an urgency ordinance.

  Councilmember LEE discussed her background with the collective bargaining process
  and the Alhambra Teachers Association, offered support for workers to receive fair
  wages and safe working conditions, and supported continued labor negotiations. She
  stated that cities such as Long Beach have expanded their authority over the wages of
  non-city employees with this ordinance, albeit with good intentions. She stated that the
  ideal solution was vaccination of all workers. She stated her preference for continued
  collective bargaining negotiations between grocery workers and their management. She

  9
2-22-21
   disagreed with the unintended consequences of cities adopting such an ordinance such
  as litigation against the city, retaliatory actions against the workers, and closure of
  stores. She awaited the outcome of the County’s decision. Ms. Lee stated that she
  wished to avoid lawsuits against the City and opposed drafting an ordinance at this time.

  Ms. PÉREZ addressed Ms. Lee’s concerns regarding labor negotiations, and stated that
  the ordinance would also include workers at large retail stores who did not have
  unionized members.

  Councilmember MAZA agreed with Ms. Lee’s sentiment, offered support for grocery
  workers, and expressed similar concerns for the City adopting the ordinance such as
  potential litigation, interfering in the collective bargaining process, pending vaccination
  access, and the desire for continued employment. He expressed preference for the City
  to wait for the County’s decision before taking action and limit exposure to liability.

  Councilmember MALONEY discussed the number of businesses which would be
  affected by the ordinance with Ms. PÉREZ, and expressed concern for smaller locally
  owned businesses. He spoke about the hardships faced by grocery workers during the
  height of the pandemic and echoed Ms. Lee’s comments regarding the need for
  compensation negotiations between workers and management. He expressed support
  for an ordinance, but stated that it needed greater clarity as to which businesses and
  workers would be affected, the exact cost of the ordinance, and whether it would
  distinguish between minimum wage workers and workers earning higher wages. He
  discussed pending litigation and the injunction as they would affect the adoption of an
  ordinance as well as the legal basis defining the urgency of the ordinance with Mr.
  MONTES. Mr. MALONEY offered support for the workers, but expressed that he wanted
  to ensure that the City approached it with the greatest care and ultimately supported
  waiting to take action until after the external discussions had resolved and after closed
  session discussion of the legal vulnerability of the City should it adopt an urgency
  ordinance.

  Ms. LEE reiterated her preference to wait to take action until after the court ruling had
  been made and the County had made their decision and expressed further concerns as
  to limiting this ordinance to grocery workers and excluding other frontline workers. Mr.
  MALONEY agreed that this ordinance was not a perfect vehicle to balance and address
  the needs of workers which warranted further discussion. Ms. PÉREZ thanked Council
  for their discussion, agreed with comments regarding the impact of outside legal
  decisions, supported further discussion, and agreed with Mr. Maza’s concerns to protect
  the City financially. She addressed comments regarding protection of other workers by
  stating that many of the groups named were already designated by the State of
  California as disaster workers but that grocery and pharmacy workers did not have the
  same distinction. She agreed with comments that the wage increase offered was
  minimal compared to the work being done, and added that Council could explore a
  minimum wage increase for all Alhambra workers. She referred to Mr. Maloney’s
  comments that this ordinance was designed to not target small business owners who
  were facing their own challenges due to the pandemic. She supported continued
  discussion. Council agreed to further discussion in closed session before the next
  regular Council meeting to the extent that there were legal updates and directed Staff to
  provide clarification as to the parameters of the ordinance and which stores would be
  impacted by the ordinance. Mr. MONTES further clarified the purpose of the pending
  injunction as it relates to defining the legality of the ordinance.

  10
2-22-21
   Action Taken:  Council agreed to further discussion in closed session before the
  next regular Council meeting to the extent that there were legal updates and directed
  staff to provide clarification as to the parameters of the ordinance and which stores
  would be impacted by the ordinance.

6.  CONSIDERATION OF A POLICE CHIEF CONTRACT WITH ERIC PARRA – F2M-71,
  F2M21-2, C2M21-8, M2M21-22

  Human Resources KO delivered a staff report. Chief of Police Timothy Vu recently
  notified the City Manager of plans to resign as of March 23, 2021. Eric Parra has
  extensive background, knowledge and experience in the field of law enforcement and
  has served as Assistant Chief of Police since 2019. In drafting the employment contract,
  staff utilized the same employment contract that was previously presented and approved
  by the City Council during the hiring of Chief of Police Timothy Vu in March 2017. The
  proposed salary and benefits were commensurate with those approved in the current
  budget.

  Discussion: Council supported the contract and praised Chief Parra for his continued
  work.

  Action Taken:  City Council approved that certain Employment Agreement
  designating Eric Parra as the Chief of Police effective March 24, 2021 on file in the
  Office of the City Clerk as Contract No. C2M21-8 and by this reference incorporated
  herein and made a part hereof as though fully set forth herein; authorized the City
  Manager to execute the Employment Agreement; and, directed staff to undertake the
  steps necessary to finalize Council’s action. (M2M21-22)

  Vote:  Moved:  MAZA  Seconded:  MALONEY
  Ayes:  MALONEY, MAZA, LEE, ANDRADE-STADLER, PÉREZ
  Noes:  NONE
  Absent:  NONE

CONSENT AGENDA (Item Nos. 7 – 18)

All items listed under the Consent Agenda, with the exception of Item No. 12, 13, and 16, were
considered by the City Council to be routine and were enacted by one motion.

16.  ADOPT A RESOLUTION APPROVING A RESIDENTIAL AND COMMERCIAL
  INTEGRATED WASTE MANAGEMENT SERVICES AGREEMENT BETWEEN THE
  CITY OF ALHAMBRA AND CONSOLIDATED DISPOSAL SERVICE, L.L.C. AND
  APPROVING CEQA EXEMPTIONS THEREFOR – F2M20-39, F2M10-26, F94-80,
  RFP2M20-10, R2M21-5, C2M21-9

  At the January 25, 2021 City Council meeting, the City Council directed staff to begin
  contract negotiations with Republic Services for a new seven-year combined residential
  and commercial integrated waste management services agreement and return to City
  Council for approval of the final contract terms. The agreement would begin on July 1,
  2021 and expire on June 30, 2028. Some of the key terms of the new combined
  residential and commercial integrated waste management services agreement with
  Republic Services were as follows: organic waste collection services; source separated
  container system; food recovery assistance; customer service and billing; extensive
  education and outreach activities to inform residential and commercial customers of new
  service levels, container configurations and recycling requirements; several
  enhancements such as a beautification program, five annual scholarships for college-
  bound seniors from any high school in Alhambra, annual food drive in conjunction with
  community-based organizations, summer internship program for Alhambra Unified
  School District (AUSD) students at Republic Services facilities, facility tours for
  community and school groups, school programs in AUSD schools and compost
  workshops for residents including homeowners’ associations; additional services such
  as backyard service for disabled cart customers, low-income discount for qualified
  customers, electronic waste (E-waste) collection, battery recycling program, sharps
  collection program, annual neighborhood clean-up, annual document shredding and
  compost giveaway event; and, compliance with multiple State laws regarding solid waste
  and recycling requirements.

  Additionally, the City reviewed the proposed adoption of an Agreement between the City
  of Alhambra and Consolidated Disposal Service, LLC, dba Republic Services, for
  Integrated Solid Waste Management Services for compliance with the California

  17
2-22-21
   Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) and based upon the recitals in this resolution, and the
  Agreement, as well as the information provided in the RFP and proposal, determined
  there was no possibility that approval of the Agreement would have a significant effect
  on the environment; therefore pursuant to Section 15061(b)(3) of the State CEQA
  Guidelines the activity is not subject to CEQA. Further, approval of the Agreement was
  exempt from CEQA pursuant to CEQA Guideline 15301(b) as the Agreement is the
  continued provision of public utility equivalent services. Finally, the approval of the
  Agreement was categorically exempt from CEQA under California Code of Regulation
  Section 15308, which exempts "actions by regulatory agencies for protection of the
  environment." The Agreement was intended to implement and is consistent with the
  goals of California State Assembly Bills 341, 939, 1594, 1826, and 2176 and Senate
  Bills 1016 and 1383.
